Recommendations for preventing infections in healthcare settings include specific work restrictions for healthcare personnel who are either exposed to or infected with significant infectious diseases. These recommendations are provided in the absence of state and local regulations. 2. 3. A list of etiologic agents responsible for community-acquired or nosocomial gastrointestinal infections in developed countries is provided, along with their epidemiological significance. 4. 5. 6. Infection control issues for healthcare personnel are comprehensively reviewed, focusing on the transmission dynamics and preventive strategies for infections in healthcare settings. 7. The updated guideline replaces the 1983 CDC Guideline for Infection Control in Hospital Personnel and provides evidence-based methods to reduce infection transmission between patients and healthcare personnel. 8. The revised guideline incorporates input from experts in infection control, occupational health, and infectious diseases, though not all recommendations may reflect unanimous agreement among reviewers. 9. The document emphasizes the epidemiology and prevention of infections transmitted in healthcare settings, supported by robust scientific data to inform recommendations. 10. 11. The guideline also addresses latex hypersensitivity issues, providing recommendations to prevent sensitization and adverse reactions among healthcare personnel due to the frequent use of latex barriers. 12. In the United States, approximately 8.8 million individuals work in healthcare professions, with about 6 million employed in over 6,000 hospitals. However, healthcare is increasingly delivered outside hospitals, such as in nursing homes, outpatient centers, emergency clinics, and patients' homes. 13. Healthcare personnel, whether hospital-based or working in other settings, may acquire infections from or transmit infections to patients, colleagues, household members, or community contacts. 14. The term healthcare personnel encompasses all paid and unpaid individuals working in healthcare settings who may be exposed to infectious materials, including body substances, contaminated medical supplies, equipment, environmental surfaces, or air. 15. Healthcare personnel include emergency medical service workers, dental personnel, laboratory staff, autopsy personnel, nurses, nursing assistants, physicians, technicians, therapists, pharmacists, students, trainees, contractual staff, and others potentially exposed to infectious agents. 16. Personnel with direct contact with patients, body fluids, or specimens face a higher risk of acquiring or transmitting infections compared to those with only brief, casual contact with patients or their environment. 17. 18. The 1983 CDC guideline focused on preventing infections transmitted to and from healthcare personnel. 19. Infection control objectives for personnel health services should be integrated into a healthcare organization's overall infection control program. 20. 21. Health inventories and physical examinations are critical components of these evaluations. 22. Immunization programs are essential for ensuring personnel immunity to vaccine-preventable diseases, preventing disease transmission, and reducing unnecessary work restrictions. Mandatory immunization programs are more effective than voluntary ones. 23. 24. 25. Maintenance of accurate, confidential health records is crucial for monitoring personnel health status, ensuring consistent services, and complying with OSHA standards for medical record retention and confidentiality. 26. The epidemiology and control of infections transmitted among healthcare personnel and patients focus on those diseases that occur frequently in healthcare settings or are of significant importance to personnel. 27. Bloodborne pathogens, such as hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV, pose significant risks in healthcare settings. 28. The risk of transmission from infected healthcare personnel to patients, particularly during invasive procedures, has been a subject of concern and debate.
